title: Fruit (and 'mortal tast')
short: Both the literal fruit of the forbidden tree and, in the Latin sense, the 'fruit' or consequence of disobedience: death and 'all our woe'.
body: The first sentence plays on two senses at once. 'Fruit' is the apple of the forbidden tree, but Milton, who habitually uses English words in their Latin root sense, also means fructus, the outcome or yield of an action: the result of Adam and Eve's disobedience is death. The next line reinforces the double meaning, since 'mortal tast' is both a taste by mortals and a 'deadly' taste (Latin mortalis); Verity glosses 'mortal' as 'deadly'. The phrase 'Brought Death into the World, and all our woe' has been heard as an echo of Virgil's comment on the union of Dido and Aeneas, 'that day was the first cause of death and woe' (Aeneid 4.169-70). The divine prohibition and its penalty come from Genesis 2:17, 'in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die', and the eating itself from Genesis 3:6. Book IX, where the fruit is finally eaten, returns repeatedly to the pun (e.g. 9.647-48, 'Fruitless to me, though Fruit be here to excess').

title: one greater Man (Christ, the second Adam)
short: Christ, the 'second Adam', whose obedience undoes the first man's disobedience (Romans 5:19).
body: The 'greater Man' is the Son of God incarnate. Milton builds the opening on Paul's contrast between Adam and Christ: 'as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous' (Romans 5:19; compare 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45). The phrase announces at the outset that the poem is not a tragedy only: loss of Eden is framed by a promised restoration, which the last two books will narrate in Michael's prophecy (12.386-465). Some editors therefore speak of two arguments in the poem, Adam's disobedience and Christ's obedience; the Dartmouth edition notes that the opening of Paradise Regained (1671) deliberately echoes these lines. 'Restore us, and regain the blissful Seat' gives Milton's later poem its title.

title: Heav'nly Muse; Oreb, Sinai
short: Milton invokes not a classical Muse but the sacred power that inspired Moses on Horeb or Sinai to write Genesis.
body: Invocation of the Muse is the conventional opening of epic (Iliad 1.1, Aeneid 1.8), but Milton redirects it. His Muse is the 'Heavenly' one who inspired 'That Shepherd' Moses (Exodus 3:1) when he received the Law on the mountain, and who was believed to have taught him the creation story he records in Genesis ('In the Beginning', the first words of both Genesis and John's Gospel). Verity notes that Scripture names the mountain both Horeb (Deuteronomy 4:10) and Sinai (Exodus 19:20), and suggests Milton leaves the choice open; the 'secret top' is the summit hidden in cloud, Latin secretus, 'set apart'. In 7.1 Milton gives this Muse the name Urania. Scholars debate whether she is simply the Holy Spirit (addressed separately at 1.17) or a distinct figure for divine wisdom; the Dartmouth edition suggests seventeenth-century readers would first have thought of the Spirit.

title: Sion Hill and Siloa's Brook
short: The hill and spring of Jerusalem by the Temple: Milton's biblical counterpart to the Muses' mountain and sacred spring.
body: Greek poets placed the Muses on Mount Helicon by the springs Aganippe and Hippocrene; Milton substitutes a sacred geography of his own. Sion (Zion) is the Temple hill of Jerusalem, and Siloa (Siloam) the spring and pool just below it, 'the waters of Shiloah that go softly' (Isaiah 8:6), where Christ sent the blind man to wash (John 9:7). The 'Oracle of God' is the sanctuary of the Temple, the Holy of Holies (Psalm 28:2). Verity explains that Milton, imitating Hesiod's opening picture of the Muses at the spring by the altar of Zeus, sets the brook beside the 'oracle' to claim the same sanctity for biblical inspiration. The detail of the healing of the blind has an obvious personal force for the blind poet, who returns to the place at 3.30-32.

title: Aonian Mount; 'Things unattempted yet in Prose or Rhime'
short: Mount Helicon in Boeotia, home of the classical Muses, which Milton's 'adventrous Song' means to soar above.
body: Aonia is an old name for Boeotia, where Mount Helicon stands; the Muses were therefore called Aonides. Milton's ambition is to fly 'with no middle flight' above it, that is, to surpass the pagan epic poets in the height of his subject. The next line, 'Things unattempted yet in Prose or Rhime', is a calculated borrowing: Ariosto opens Orlando Furioso (1.2) promising 'cosa non detta in prosa mai né in rima', things never said in prose or rhyme. Readers have found irony in the claim to novelty being itself a quotation, and in borrowing it from a light-hearted romance. 'Rhime' here simply means verse, though Milton's prefatory note on 'The Verse' famously rejects rhyme for heroic poetry. The image of a soaring flight that might fall is picked up again in the invocation to Book VII (7.12-20), where Bellerophon's fall is the warning.

title: Dove-like satst brooding
short: The Holy Spirit at the Creation, pictured as a bird brooding on eggs, conflating Genesis 1:2 with the dove of Christ's baptism.
body: Genesis 1:2 says the Spirit of God 'moved upon the face of the waters'. Verity explains that the Hebrew verb can mean 'fluttered' or 'brooded' like a bird hatching eggs, the sense several Latin Fathers adopted; Milton chooses brooding, and makes the image physical: the Spirit 'mad'st it pregnant'. The dove comes from the Gospels, where the Spirit descends 'in a bodily shape like a dove' at Christ's baptism (Luke 3:22). The Dartmouth edition points out how far Milton pushes the generative image: creation is pictured almost as a fertilising of the unformed matter of Chaos, consistent with his view (set out in his Christian Doctrine) that God made the world not from nothing but out of a matter that came from himself. Compare the account of creation in 7.234-37.

title: Argument; assert
short: 'Argument' means the subject or theme of the poem, as in Latin argumentum; to 'assert' Providence is to defend or vindicate it.
body: Milton uses 'Argument' in its Latin and Renaissance sense of subject matter, as in the prose 'Arguments' prefaced to each book; Verity glosses it 'subject = Lat. argumentum' and compares 9.28-29, where Milton calls the fall a 'Subject' and his theme an argument 'Not less but more Heroic' than Homer's. Likewise 'assert' (1.25) does not mean merely 'state' but, as Verity notes, 'vindicate', from the Latin assertor, one who claims a person's freedom in law: Milton undertakes to champion God's providence against its accusers. The word 'highth' (height) frames the task as an ascent, continuing the flight imagery of 1.13-15.

title: justifie the wayes of God to men
short: The poem's stated aim is a theodicy: to show that God is just in allowing the Fall and in his dealings with humankind.
body: This line states the poem's purpose as theodicy, the defence of divine justice in a world containing evil. Verity compares the chorus of Milton's Samson Agonistes, 'Just are the ways of God, And justifiable to men' (293-94), and scriptural phrasing such as 'just and true are thy ways' (Revelation 15:3; Psalm 145:17). Pope echoed the line in his Essay on Man, 'vindicate the ways of God to man' (1.16). How far the poem succeeds is one of the oldest debates about it: the Father's long self-justification in Book III (80-134), insisting that angels and humans were made 'Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall', is the central exhibit. Readers from Blake and Shelley to William Empson (Milton's God, 1961) have argued that the poem's God is less sympathetic than its Satan; others answer that the reader's own fallen sympathies are part of what the poem tests.

title: Adamantine Chains
greek: Greek adamas, 'unconquerable', hence the hardest metal or stone
short: Unbreakable chains: the classical adamant of Tartarus joined to the 'chains of darkness' that bind the fallen angels in 2 Peter and Jude.
body: Adamant (Greek adamas, 'untameable') was the fabulous hardest substance of classical poetry: Virgil's Tartarus has pillars of solid adamant (Aeneid 6.552), and Aeschylus' Prometheus is fastened with adamantine bonds. Milton combines this with Scripture: God 'spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness' (2 Peter 2:4; compare Jude 6 and Revelation 20:1-2). Verity collects the later references (2.169, 2.183, 2.196). There is a deliberate tension here, since Satan in fact rises freely from the lake a few lines later; the narrator explains at 1.210-20 that he is loosed only by 'the will And high permission of all-ruling Heaven', so that the chains are as much a figure of divine control as literal fetters.

title: Nine times the Space (nine days)
short: The rebels lie stunned nine days, recalling Hesiod's Titans, whose fall from heaven to earth and from earth to Tartarus each took nine days.
body: Hesiod measures the depth of Tartarus by a falling bronze anvil, which would drop for nine days and nights from heaven and reach earth on the tenth, and fall as long again from earth to Tartarus (Theogony 722-25). Milton uses the number twice: the angels lie vanquished on the fiery gulf for nine days here, and Raphael later says their fall from Heaven itself lasted 'Nine dayes' (6.871). Verity notes that nine, as the square of three, was traditionally significant. The allusion is part of Milton's systematic identification of the fallen angels with the Titans and Giants who rebelled against Zeus (1.197-200), myths he treats as distorted pagan memories of the true war in Heaven.

title: No light, but rather darkness visible
short: A famous oxymoron: Hell's fire gives no light, only a gloom that makes its horrors dimly visible.
body: The phrase is an oxymoron, a figure that joins contradictory terms. Verity explains the conception: not total blackness, in which the 'sights of woe' could not be seen, but a gloom which half reveals and half conceals. It drew on an old belief, reported by Basil and others, that hellfire burns without shining. Job had described the land of the dead as a place 'where the light is as darkness' (Job 10:22). The paradox also suits a poem whose narrator is blind and which treats inner and outer light as opposed (3.51-55). Pope parodied the line in the Dunciad (4.1-4), and William Styron borrowed it as the title for his memoir of depression (1990). The following line, 'hope never comes That comes to all', echoes the inscription over Dante's gate of Hell (Inferno 3.9).

title: Beelzebub
short: Satan's second-in-command, named after the Philistine god of Ekron, 'lord of flies', called 'prince of the devils' in the Gospels.
body: Baal-zebub was the god of Ekron consulted by King Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:2); the name is traditionally explained as 'lord of flies'. In the Gospels Beelzebub is 'the prince of the devils' (Matthew 12:24; Luke 11:15), effectively another name for Satan, but Milton makes him a separate figure, Satan's confidant and next in rank, as the Argument says ('next in Order and Dignity'). Satan later reminds him that he was the first to hear of the rebellion (5.673-79). In the council of Book II Beelzebub proposes, as if his own, the plan Satan has already devised: the attack on the new world and on mankind (2.310-78). Verity notes that Milton returns to his name at 1.271 and that the catalogue explains how the fallen angels later acquired the names of pagan gods.

title: Satan ('adversary')
short: The Hebrew word means 'adversary'; Milton says the name was given to him only after his revolt, his former name being erased.
body: In Hebrew satan means an adversary or accuser, as in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3:1, where 'the satan' is a member of the heavenly court. The phrase 'thence in Heav'n call'd Satan' stresses that this is a new name earned by the rebellion; Book V says his 'former name Is heard no more in Heav'n' (5.658-59). Verity notes that it is uncertain whether that former name was Lucifer, the 'day star' of Isaiah 14:12 which Christian tradition applied to Satan; Milton uses 'Lucifer' later (7.131-33, 10.425) but seems to treat it, like Satan, as a post-rebellion title. The erasure of the rebels' heavenly names is a recurring idea (1.361-63, 6.373-80): they are known only by the names men later gave them as idols.

title: But O how fall'n! how chang'd
short: Satan's first words combine Isaiah's taunt over the fallen 'Lucifer' with Aeneas' cry at the mangled ghost of Hector.
body: Verity identifies a double allusion. Isaiah's song over the king of Babylon, 'How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!' (Isaiah 14:12), was traditionally read as describing Satan's fall. In Virgil, Aeneas dreams of Hector's mutilated ghost and exclaims 'quantum mutatus ab illo / Hectore', 'how changed from that Hector' who returned in triumph (Aeneid 2.274-75). Put in Satan's mouth and addressed to Beelzebub, the scriptural words become unconsciously self-describing: the speaker cannot see that the lament applies to himself. The broken syntax, 'If thou beest he', begun and never completed (Verity calls it an anacoluthon), expresses agitation.

title: Titanian, Earth-born; Briareos and Typhon
short: Satan's bulk is compared with the monstrous rebels against Zeus: the hundred-handed Briareos and the serpent-giant Typhon.
body: The first epic simile for Satan sets him beside the rebels of Greek myth. The Titans, children of Heaven and Earth, warred against Zeus (Jove) and were hurled into Tartarus; the 'Earth-born' Giants made a later assault. Briareos, the hundred-handed son of Uranus, stands in for the first group; Typhon (Typhoeus), the many-headed serpent-monster whom Zeus blasted with his thunderbolt and buried under Etna (Hesiod, Theogony 820-68), for the second. 'The Den By ancient Tarsus' recalls Pindar and Aeschylus, who placed Typhon in a Cilician cave (Prometheus Bound 351-54), as Verity notes. Milton's word 'fables' in 1.197 is significant: classical myth is treated as a garbled memory of the true rebellion in Heaven. The comparison, though grand, places Satan among defeated monsters.

title: Leviathan (the whale-island simile)
short: Satan lies like the sea-beast Leviathan, which sailors mistake for an island and moor to, to their ruin: an image of deceptive security.
body: Leviathan is the sea-monster of Job 41 and Isaiah 27:1 ('Leviathan the piercing serpent'), read in Milton's day as the whale. Verity notes that the Hebrew word could also mean other huge creatures, such as the crocodile. The simile draws on the bestiary and traveller's tale of the whale mistaken for an island, on which sailors anchor or land until it dives; Verity cites the version in Olaus Magnus' History of the Northern Nations. The tale was traditionally moralised as the devil deceiving careless souls, so the comparison works as a warning: the 'Pilot of some small night-founder'd Skiff' trusting the beast is like the reader, or Eve, who finds Satan's greatness reassuring. The simile also sets up Satan's later disguises, and is echoed in the creation of the whale at 7.412-16.

anchor: The mind is its own place
title: The mind is its own place; Better to reign in Hell
short: Satan's boast that the mind creates its own heaven or hell, and that rule in Hell is better than service in Heaven, is answered later by his own despair.
body: Satan claims a Stoic self-sufficiency (Verity, citing Thyer, notes the Stoic colouring): an unconquered mind 'Can make a Heav'n of Hell, a Hell of Heav'n'. The boast is ironically fulfilled in Book IV, when he discovers 'Which way I flie is Hell; my self am Hell' (4.75): the mind is indeed its own place, but his is a hell he carries everywhere. Verity compares Mephistophilis in Marlowe's Doctor Faustus: 'where we are is hell'. The next famous line, 'Better to reign in Hell, then serve in Heav'n' (1.263), inverts the words of Akhilleus' ghost in the Odyssey, who would rather be a poor man's hired labourer on earth than king over all the dead (Odyssey 11.489-91). Abdiel's answer to the slogan comes, chronologically earlier, at 6.178-83.

title: Optic Glass; the Tuscan Artist (Galileo)
short: Galileo, whose telescope revealed the moon's mountains; the only contemporary Milton names in the poem (at 5.262).
body: Satan's shield is compared to the moon as seen through the 'Optic Glass' (telescope) of Galileo, the Tuscan astronomer, observing from Fiesole ('Fesole') or the valley of the Arno ('Valdarno') near Florence. Verity points out that Galileo did not invent the telescope but developed it, and that Milton visited him in 1638-39, when the old astronomer was under house arrest by the Inquisition; Milton recalls the visit in Areopagitica as an example of censorship crushing learning. Galileo is the one modern figure named in the poem (5.262; again implied at 3.588-90). The simile is double-edged: it magnifies Satan's shield to planetary size, yet the 'spotty Globe' suggests blemish, and the uncertainty of what the lens reveals anticipates the astronomical debates of Book VIII.

title: Thick as Autumnal Leaves ... In Vallombrosa
short: The fallen legions lie as thick as autumn leaves on the streams of Vallombrosa near Florence: an ancient simile for the multitudes of the dead.
body: The leaf-simile for countless souls is one of the oldest in epic: Homer compares the generations of men to leaves (Iliad 6.146-49), Virgil the dead crowding to Charon's boat to leaves falling in the first frost of autumn (Aeneid 6.309-10), and Dante the damned to autumn leaves dropping one by one (Inferno 3.112-15). Milton localises it in Vallombrosa ('shady valley'), a wooded valley with a famous monastery some eighteen miles from Florence, which he may have visited in 1638. Verity notes that its beech and chestnut woods and many streams fit the picture exactly. 'Etrurian shades' suggests both shady woods and the 'shades' of the dead. The simile then slides into another, of sedge (seaweed) scattered on the Red Sea, preparing the image of drowned Egyptians.

title: Busiris and his Memphian Chivalrie
short: Milton names the Pharaoh drowned in the Red Sea 'Busiris', a tyrant king of Egypt in Greek legend; 'Memphian' means Egyptian.
body: The simile turns from leaves to sedge floating on the Red Sea (the Hebrew Yam Suph, 'sea of reeds', as the Dartmouth note observes), and then to the Egyptian army drowned there while pursuing the Israelites, 'the Sojourners of Goshen' (Exodus 14). Busiris was, in Greek writers such as Isocrates, a cruel Egyptian king killed by Hercules; Verity observes that no one has explained why Milton gives his name to the Pharaoh of the Exodus, and suggests Milton either followed an unknown authority or used the name as a general title like 'Pharaoh'. 'Memphian', from Memphis, means Egyptian, and 'Chivalrie' cavalry. The point of the comparison is moral as well as visual: the fallen angels, like Pharaoh's host, are a tyrant's army destroyed for pursuing God's people, and Orion, the stormy constellation (Aeneid 1.535), presides over their wreck.

title: Moloch
short: The Ammonite god to whom children were sacrificed by fire; first in the catalogue because fiercest, he speaks for open war in Book II.
body: The catalogue of devils (1.376-521) imitates Homer's Catalogue of Ships (Iliad 2.484 ff.) but names the fallen angels by the idols men later worshipped. Moloch (Hebrew melek, 'king', hence Milton's 'horrid King') was 'the abomination of the children of Ammon' (1 Kings 11:7), to whom children were 'passed through the fire' (2 Kings 23:10). Verity quotes George Sandys' Relation (1615), Milton's likely source, describing a hollow brass idol heated red within while drums and timbrels drowned the children's cries. Solomon built him a shrine on the Mount of Olives (the 'opprobrious Hill'), and his rites in the valley of Hinnom made that valley's name, Gehenna, a 'Type of Hell' (1.404-05; Jeremiah 19:6). In Book II Moloch is the advocate of open war (2.51-105).

title: Chemos (Chemosh) and Peor
short: The god of Moab, identified with Baal-Peor, at whose rites in Shittim Israel sinned and was punished with plague.
body: Chemosh was 'the abomination of Moab' (1 Kings 11:7; Numbers 21:29), for whom Solomon also built a high place. Milton follows the identification, noted by Verity, of Chemos with Baal-Peor, the Moabite Baal worshipped on Mount Peor. At Shittim ('Sittim') the Israelites, 'on thir march from Nile', joined in the rites of Baal-Peor with the women of Moab and a plague killed twenty-four thousand (Numbers 25:1-9), hence 'wanton rites, which cost them woe'. The epithet 'obscene' refers to the sexual character Milton attributes to the cult. The place-names (Aroer, Nebo, Heshbon, Sibma, Elealè) trace the territory east of the Dead Sea, the 'Asphaltic Pool'. Verity notes that Milton once listed 'Moabitides' among possible subjects for a sacred drama.

title: Baalim and Ashtaroth; the sex of spirits
short: Plural titles for the many local forms of Baal and Astarte, and Milton's claim that spirits can take either sex at will.
body: Baal ('lord') was the chief male god of the Canaanites and Phoenicians, worshipped under many local titles (Baal-Peor, Baal-zebub, Baal-berith); 'Baalim' is the Hebrew plural for all of them, and 'Ashtaroth' likewise for the forms of the goddess Ashtoreth (Verity). The plural lets Milton add a striking piece of angelology: 'Spirits when they please Can either Sex assume, or both' (1.423-24), because their 'Essence pure' is not tied to limbs and joints. The idea prepares for the shape-shifting of the devils in the poem and for Raphael's account of angelic love in 8.615-29. Verity notes that Pope turned the passage to comedy in The Rape of the Lock (1.69-70). The angels' bodies are one of the poem's acknowledged difficulties, as Dr Johnson observed.

title: Astoreth (Astarte), Queen of Heaven
short: The Phoenician moon-goddess of Sidon, 'Queen of Heav'n', worshipped by Solomon under the influence of his foreign wives.
body: Ashtoreth, called Astarte by the Greeks, was the great goddess of the Phoenicians, cognate with the Babylonian Ishtar and often identified with Aphrodite. Verity explains that she was associated with the moon and shown with crescent horns, hence 'crescent Horns' and her title 'Queen of Heav'n' (Jeremiah 7:18, 44:17); Milton's Nativity Ode calls her 'mooned Ashtaroth'. Solomon, the 'uxorious King' whose 'heart, though large' was led astray by his foreign wives, built her a temple on the 'offensive Mountain', the Mount of Olives (1 Kings 11:4-5; 2 Kings 23:13). The Dartmouth note observes that Milton, like the biblical writers, links sexual infidelity with idolatry, a connection that bears on the poem's treatment of Adam's choice in Book IX.

title: Thammuz (Adonis)
short: The dying god mourned by the women of Jerusalem, identified with Adonis, whose river reddened each year as if with his blood.
body: Ezekiel saw 'women weeping for Tammuz' at the gate of the Temple (Ezekiel 8:14). Milton identifies him, as was usual, with Adonis, the youth of Byblos killed by a boar on Lebanon and lamented each year. Verity explains the 'yearly wounded' detail: the river Adonis ran red each spring with mud washed down from the mountains, which worshippers took to be his blood renewed. The myth of death and revival symbolised the seasons. Milton presents the cult as a contagious 'Love-tale' that 'Infected Sions daughters with like heat', moving from Syria to the very porch of the Temple; the 'dark Idolatries Of alienated Judah' are those Ezekiel saw in vision. Adonis returns in the poem's Eden, where the garden is compared to the 'Gardens of Adonis' (9.439-40).

title: Dagon
short: The Philistine god, half man, half fish, whose image fell maimed before the captured Ark of the Covenant.
body: Dagon was the national god of the Philistines. When they placed the captured Ark in his temple at Ashdod, his image was found fallen on its face, its head and hands broken off on the threshold ('grunsel'), so that 'he maim'd his brute Image' (1 Samuel 5:1-5). Milton follows the traditional derivation from Hebrew dag, 'fish', making him a merman ('upward Man And downward Fish'); Verity notes the alternative derivation from the word for corn, and that Assyrian inscriptions name a god Dagan. The five Philistine cities listed (Azotus/Ashdod, Gath, Ascalon, Accaron/Ekron, Gaza) appear in the Septuagint or Vulgate forms Milton preferred. Dagon is the god whose feast Samson destroys in Milton's Samson Agonistes.

title: Rimmon
short: The god of Damascus, whose worshipper Naaman was healed in the Jordan, and to whose altar King Ahaz conformed the Temple.
body: Rimmon was the god of Damascus, 'the house of Rimmon' where Naaman the Syrian bowed with his king (2 Kings 5:18); scholars identify him with the storm-god Hadad. Damascus lay on the 'lucid streams' of Abbana and Pharphar, the rivers Naaman preferred to the Jordan until Elisha's command cured his leprosy (2 Kings 5:12-14): so Rimmon 'lost' a worshipper, 'A Leper once he lost'. But he 'gain'd a King', Ahaz of Judah, who copied an altar from Damascus and set it in the Temple in place of God's (2 Kings 16:10-16), worshipping 'the gods whom he had vanquished'. Verity notes Milton's correct stress on 'Abbana'. The pattern of the catalogue is clear: each idol is placed where it most offended against Israel's God.

title: Osiris, Isis, Orus and the golden calf
greek: Egyptian gods; Apis, the sacred bull
short: The animal-shaped gods of Egypt, whose bull-cult Milton traces in Israel's golden calf and Jeroboam's two calves.
body: Osiris, his consort Isis and their son Horus ('Orus') head the Egyptian pantheon, whose gods were worshipped in 'brutish forms'. Verity explains that Osiris was venerated in the sacred bull Apis, and Milton follows a long tradition in tracing to this the golden calf that Aaron made in the wilderness (Exodus 32), the 'Calf in Oreb'. The 'Rebel King' Jeroboam 'doubl'd that sin' by setting up two golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28-29), and Psalm 106:20 mocks those who changed their glory 'into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass'. The final line recalls the tenth plague, when God 'equal'd with one stroke Both her first born and all her bleating Gods' (Exodus 12:12, which threatens judgment on 'all the gods of Egypt').

title: Belial
short: Not originally a god but a Hebrew word for worthlessness ('sons of Belial'); Milton makes him the spirit of lust, luxury and court debauchery.
body: Verity points out that Belial was never the name of a god: the Hebrew word means 'worthlessness', and 'sons of Belial' simply means scoundrels, like the corrupt priests, the sons of Eli (1 Samuel 2:12), or the men of Gibeah whose assault on the Levite's concubine Milton recalls (Judges 19:22-28), with the parallel story of Sodom (Genesis 19). Milton turns the abstraction into a person: no temple stands to him, yet he is everywhere, in churches, 'Courts and Palaces' and 'luxurious Cities'. The reference to riotous 'Sons Of Belial, flown with insolence and wine' was readily applied to the court and streets of Restoration London, and Verity notes the boldness of the line under Charles II. In Book II Belial argues smoothly for 'ignoble ease' (2.119-228).

title: Azazel
short: Satan's standard-bearer, named from the mysterious Azazel to whom the scapegoat was sent on the Day of Atonement.
body: In Leviticus 16:8-10 one of two goats on the Day of Atonement is chosen by lot 'for Azazel' and sent into the wilderness bearing the people's sins; the King James Version translates the word as 'scapegoat', while the margin keeps 'Azazel'. Verity notes that the word is now widely taken to name a demon of the desert, and suggests that Milton followed medieval demonologists in making him a fallen angel; in the apocryphal Book of Enoch Azazel is a leader of the rebel angels who taught men weapons and adornment. Milton gives him the honour of carrying Satan's 'Imperial Ensign', which, when unfurled, 'Shon like a Meteor streaming to the Wind'. The irony of the scapegoat bearing the rebels' banner is left implicit.

title: the Dorian mood of Flutes and soft Recorders
greek: Greek harmonia Dôristi, the Dorian mode
short: The grave Greek musical mode associated with courage; the devils march like Spartans, steadied by flutes.
body: The fallen angels advance 'In perfect Phalanx to the Dorian mood Of Flutes and soft Recorders', a picture Verity traces to Thucydides' description of the Spartans moving into battle at Mantinea slowly, to the music of many flute-players (Thucydides 5.70). The Dorian was the 'manly' Greek mode: Plato in the Republic keeps it as the music of courage while banishing the softer Lydian, and Aristotle (Politics 8) praises its steadying effect. Milton himself argued in Of Education that music shapes character. The music here works on the devils as true discipline might, 'Breathing united force' and assuaging their pain, which makes it one of several passages where their heroism is genuinely impressive even as it serves a false cause.

title: Uthers Son and the heroes of romance
short: Satan's army outnumbers every host of epic and romance, from Thebes and Troy to Arthur and Charlemagne's peers.
body: After the catalogue, Milton measures the devils' army against all of literature's armies: the Giants at Phlegra, the heroes of Thebes and Ilium, King Arthur ('Uthers Son', son of Uther Pendragon), and the knights of the Italian and French romances who jousted at Aspramont, Montalban and Trebizond, and Charlemagne whose peers fell 'By Fontarabbia'. Verity notes that in his Latin Epitaphium Damonis the young Milton had planned an Arthurian epic; the list is therefore partly a farewell to subjects he chose not to write. The legends are relegated to 'Fable or Romance'. The line on Charlemagne is a crux: in the familiar story Roland and the rearguard fell at Roncesvalles, and Charlemagne himself survived, so editors have suggested that Milton followed a variant chronicle or romance tradition.

title: the Sun in dim Eclips ... Perplexes Monarchs
short: Satan's dimmed glory is compared to an eclipsed sun that frightens kings with fear of change: lines the licenser nearly censored.
body: Satan's form 'had yet not lost All her Original brightness' and is compared to the rising sun seen through mist or to the sun in eclipse, which 'with fear of change Perplexes Monarchs'. Eclipses were traditionally omens of disaster for rulers. Verity records that these are the lines the official licenser is said to have objected to when the poem was submitted for publication; the story derives from John Toland's Life of Milton (1698), which says the licenser almost suppressed the poem on their account. In 1667, seven years after the Restoration of Charles II, a regicide's talk of the fall of monarchs could hardly be innocent. The simile is also theologically exact: Satan is a fading light, not darkness itself, and his brightness declines through the poem (compare 4.835-40).

title: Mammon
short: Aramaic 'wealth', personified; even in Heaven he looked down at the golden pavement rather than up at God.
body: Mammon is not a god's name but an Aramaic word for riches, as in 'Ye cannot serve God and mammon' (Matthew 6:24); Verity notes it was treated as a proper name, and Spenser had already made him a character, the god of wealth in his underground cave (Faerie Queene 2.7). Milton's Mammon is 'the least erected Spirit that fell', using 'erected' in the Latin sense of 'upright, elevated': in Heaven he admired the 'trod'n Gold' of the pavement (Revelation 21:21) more than the vision of God. He leads the mining of the hill, teaching men later to 'Ransack'd the Center', and the narrator's comment 'Let none admire That riches grow in Hell' is pointed satire. In Book II Mammon proposes building a rival empire in Hell (2.229-83).

title: Mulciber (Vulcan, Hephaestus)
short: The architect of Pandaemonium is the classical smith-god, whose famous fall from heaven to Lemnos Milton calls a pagan error.
body: The architect of Pandaemonium was known in Heaven by another name; men called him Mulciber, a Latin title of Vulcan (Greek Hephaestus), explained by Verity as 'the softener' or welder of metal. The lines on his fall translate and expand Iliad 1.590-94, where Hephaestus tells how Zeus threw him from heaven and he fell all day, landing on Lemnos at sunset: 'from Morn To Noon he fell, from Noon to dewy Eve, A Summers day'. The slow, lovely rhythm makes the fall beautiful, and then Milton cancels it: 'thus they relate, Erring; for he with this rebellious rout Fell long before'. The passage shows Milton's method of absorbing classical myth while denying its truth; Verity notes that the young Milton had used the same story in two Latin poems.

title: Pandaemonium
short: Milton's coinage, 'the place of all the demons': Satan's capital, built in an hour like an exhalation, with the splendour of a baroque temple.
body: The word is Milton's own invention from Greek pan ('all') and daimon ('spirit', in Christian use 'demon'), modelled on words like Pantheon, the temple of all the gods; Verity and the Dartmouth edition both note the coinage. Its general sense of noisy chaos came only later. The building 'Rose like an Exhalation' to music (1.711-12), a parody of creation, and its Doric pillars, architrave, fretted gold roof and lamps of naphtha recall a classical temple or St Peter's in Rome; Milton says neither Babylon nor Egypt's Memphis ever matched it. The work of a single hour outdoes the labours of ages, which the narrator offers as a lesson for those who 'boast' of human monuments such as Babel and the pyramids. The 'secret conclave' at the end of the book glances at the election of a pope.

title: As Bees in spring time
short: The crowding devils are like bees swarming about their hive, a simile from Homer and Virgil that also prepares for their shrinking.
body: Homer compares the Greeks pouring out to assembly to swarms of bees (Iliad 2.87-90), and Virgil the Carthaginians building their city to bees at work in early summer (Aeneid 1.430-36); Verity notes both models and the hissing sibilants of 'Brusht with the hiss of russling wings', which anticipate the devils' hiss as serpents in Book X. The bees 'expatiate and confer Thir State affairs', a mock-political touch. The simile also prepares a startling change of scale: to fit inside the hall, the devils shrink to the size of pygmies or 'Faerie Elves' while their leaders keep their own size. The diminution is comic and sinister at once, and ironically repeats Satan's later transformations.

title: Pigmean Race ... Faerie Elves ... belated Peasant
short: The shrunken devils resemble pygmies or fairies glimpsed by a peasant who 'sees, Or dreams he sees' them dancing by moonlight.
body: The pygmies dwelt, according to Pliny (Natural History 7.26), in the mountains beyond the source of the Ganges, which Verity identifies with the 'Indian Mount' (Imaus) and the Dartmouth edition also cites; Homer pictures their war with the cranes (Iliad 3.3-7). The fairies come from English folklore and from A Midsummer Night's Dream, which Milton echoes. The 'belated Peasant' who 'sees, Or dreams he sees' borrows Virgil's description of Aeneas glimpsing Dido's shade as one who 'sees or thinks he has seen the moon through clouds' (Aeneid 6.454). The uncertainty matters: the reader, like the peasant, is left unsure what the devils really are, and the moon, the 'Arbitress' or witness, 'Wheels her pale course' nearer the earth, as if drawn down by magic.
